addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

# Todo

This file contains near term tasks with a short description
and reference links to more details.

Intro paragraphs in `## Todo` and `## Bugs` should begin every
line with 1 leading space so they don't match the `^\d+\. `
pattern that locates numbered entries; 2 or 3 spaces also work.

## In Progress

A cycle's record has one home at a time, and while the cycle runs this is it. At Preparation
the picked-up `## Todo` item **moves** here (never copied, one home per text) and becomes six
provisional items, all required, all revised as steps land. At close-out the whole block moves
into `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` and becomes that cycle's `##` section. It is never written in
two places. Shape:

```
### <type>: <title>

#### Problem
<what is wrong, a sentence or two>

#### Solution
<what will be done about it, broad; provisional until the close-out>

#### Acceptance check
<the measure of "are you finished?">

#### Ladder
- [[N]] [<cycle title> opening][M] (done)
- [[N]] [<title>][M] (current)
- [[N]] [<title>][M]
- [[N]] <cycle title> closing

#### Deliberation
<how the five above were decided; `_None._` if there was nothing to deliberate>

#### Ladder details
<one `#####` subsection per rung, headed by its exact title, opened at laddering with the
rung's intent and completed at landing with the conceptual delta; the closing rung's only at
close-out, gotchas in problem/solution form>
```

A multi-cycle program adds one level: the program is the `###`, its current cycle the `####`,
and the six items sit one level below that (headings give the current work durable anchors,
which numbered Todo entries can't). Full rules in
[cycle-protocol.md](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#preparation); the move's four transforms are
in [Chores sections](agent-data/cycle-protocol.md#chores-sections).

### docs: freshen vc-config and config subcmd

#### Problem

Both repos' `.vc-config.toml` carry a fossil `[push]` comment block from an older binary's
schema, the retired `.vc-x1` state dirs linger (empty dirs on disk, a `/.vc-x1` line in the
work `.gitignore`), generated config comments have no refresh tooling so they rot silently, and
the bot dir's `.claude` name is agent-specific where this workspace wants the neutral
`.agent-session`. Underneath those, the toml format itself caps the doc story: a `#` comment
block linkifies nothing, so a reader cannot click from a key to its documentation.

# custom-family.md - vc-x1's layer, as a member of the vc-x1 agent-file family

Read after [custom.md](custom.md), whose single convention entry points here. Present only in a
member repo. A project that is not a member does not carry this file, and nothing in it applies
to one.

**A member's `custom.md` differs from the payload by that one line, and everything of its own lives
here.** That is the family's convention and it buys a property worth having: `diff custom.md
<template>/work/custom.md` is one line for every member, so the file that can never be pinned still
converges, and a member's whole customization surface is this file. The medium below is here for
that reason rather than because it has anything to do with the family.

## Medium and validation

The artifact is the `vc-x1` CLI, a Rust crate (manifest `Cargo.toml`, package name `vc-x1`).
Versioning specifics are in [versioning.md](agent-data/versioning.md).

**What a version bump promises**: `X.Y.Z` is a scope signal to readers of the history (see
[Advancing X.Y.Z](agent-data/versioning.md#advancing-xyz-scope-decides)), not a compatibility
contract. The crate has no library target, but the built CLI has external consumers (the family's
repos run it), so a change that breaks an existing invocation or the `.vc-config.toml` schema is
called out in the commit and surfaced by the tool's own errors rather than promised by the
version. Revisit with a compat clause if a library crate ever splits out.

**Single-name convention** (adopted at the 0.78.3 cycle): the package name is the binary's
name, `vc-x1` on `main`, with per-line dev names on long-lived branches, guarded by `build.rs`
on every cargo verb. This is the project's answer to versioning.md's
[Dev artifact name](agent-data/versioning.md#dev-artifact-name): the repo is striving to
release, so `main` builds install as plain `vc-x1`.

- **Full validation**
  - when: per-commit checklist step 5 (skip-able for notes-only commits, mandatory at close-out)
  - run as separate invocations, each exit status checked:
    1. `cargo fmt`
    2. `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`
    3. `cargo test`
    4. `cargo install --path . --locked`
    5. (re-test if anything substantive changed)
- **Fast validation**
  - when: ladder checklist step 3
  - `cargo test --bins`

## Membership

- **member name**: `vc-x1`
- **template repository**: `../vc-x1-template`

These two are environment rather than instruction, the same species as `.vc-config.toml`'s
`[repos]` paths, and they belong there instead. They cannot move yet: `vc-x1 config --validate`
rejects keys it does not know, so a config carrying them would fail its own validator. The
`[private]` table proposal tracks the fix.

## Messaging

Members leave word for each other in per-member mailboxes at the template repository. The protocol
is `../vc-x1-template/MESSAGES.md` and it governs. These are the parts that decide how a session
behaves.

- **At acquaint, check `../vc-x1-template/messages/vc-x1.md`.** An absent file means no mail.
- **Handle, then delete** the entry, and delete the file once it empties. Mailboxes hold open
  items only.
- **So a message can never be a record.** Anything in one worth keeping is copied into
  `notes/chores/chores-NN.md` *before* the entry is deleted.
- **An incoming request becomes a Todo or backlog entry, and the reply cites it** (wink,
  2026-08-12, interim practice). A message is deleted when handled, so a request living only
  in a mailbox has no home the moment it is answered, and a commit has nothing to reference.
  An entry outlives both. Interim pending todo-backlog's **What carries a Todo entry: numbered
  list, heading, or a tracker outside the repo?**, whose tracker option would serve this
  directly.
  - **the archive the protocol names does not exist yet.** MESSAGES.md says the recipient may
    delete a handled entry because "jj history is the archive", but the template repo's `main`
    is a single `Initial commit` holding `.gitignore` and `.vc-config.toml`; every mailbox,
    MESSAGES.md itself, and the whole `work/` payload are uncommitted working copy. So a
    deletion today is unrecoverable, and copying out first is the only thing standing between
    a handled message and its loss.
- **Messages are thin pointers, not state.** Durable coordination state lives in topical files. A
  message says "action needed, see <file>" rather than restating the details.
- **Write to a member's mailbox, never into their repo.** A repo with a live session is written
  only by its own agent.

## Dogfood log

This project's log lives in [notes/dogfood.md](notes/dogfood.md): dated entries on where the
pinned instructions chafed, failed, or got amended, the evidence base for the family's
convergence decisions ([Changing the agent-files](AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)). It stays
a separate file because it predates this one and is long. In-flight entries only: a resolved
entry retires at the beat where it resolves, per
[Retiring Done entries](agent-data/notes.md#retiring-done-entries).

Configure the work-repo of a dual repo system. The other repo, we call the agent-repo, is
also a markdown configuration file typically named .vc-config.md.

The code blocks in these config files are in toml format and these blocks are logically
concatenated in the order written here and those become the information used for configuring
the system. The [vc-config.md](vc-config.md) contains the documentation for the
various toml tables used for configuration and it is also used during compilation to define
the valid contents of this file.

The file [vc-config-test.md](vc-config-test.md) is a simple version of this file.
(I think we might rename the file vc-config-test.md to vc-config-model.md and it should
also contain every table and key/value pair showing typical or default values, my thoughts)

The two repos
- work [[1]]
- bot [[2]]

[repos]
work = "."
bot = ".claude"
```

[1]: vc-config.md#reposwork

856	                        "--scope=bot: no bot repo configured. Add `bot = \"...\"` to the \
857	                         [repos] registry to enable dual-repo operations",
858	                    )?;
859	                repos.push(resolve_repo_path(root, bot));
860	            }
861	        }
862	    }
863	    Ok(repos)
864	}
865	
866	/// Resolve the workspace's bot-repo path, or `None` when it has no
867	/// bot side.
868	///
869	/// The scope-aware prelude for commands that *optionally* work
870	/// against the bot repo (validate-desc / fix-desc): topology comes
871	/// from `default_scope` (the workspace config), not a flag:
872	/// `Ok(None)` means a POR / single-repo workspace, the caller's
873	/// no-op case, while a configured-but-broken bot side still errors
874	/// via `scope_to_repos`.
875	pub fn bot_repo_path(workspace_root: &Path) -> Result<Option<PathBuf>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
876	    match configured_bot_dir(workspace_root)? {
877	        Some(bot) => {
878	            verify_workspace_coherence(workspace_root, &bot)?;
879	            Ok(Some(bot))
880	        }
881	        None => Ok(None),
882	    }
883	}
884	
885	/// The bot dir the workspace config *declares*: a pure config
886	/// read, no on-disk verification.
887	///
888	/// The pre-coherence half of [`bot_repo_path`], for callers that
889	/// resolve the dir before it exists (clone names the local clone
890	/// destination from the just-cloned work repo's config). `Ok(None)`
891	/// when the workspace declares no bot side.
892	pub fn configured_bot_dir(
893	    workspace_root: &Path,
894	) -> Result<Option<PathBuf>, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
895	    reject_legacy_config(workspace_root)?;
896	    if !default_scope(Some(workspace_root)).has_bot() {
897	        return Ok(None);
898	    }
899	    let repos = scope_to_repos(&Scope(vec![Side::Bot]), Some(workspace_root))?;
900	    match repos.as_slice() {
901	        [bot] => Ok(Some(bot.clone())),
902	        other => Err(format!(
903	            "configured_bot_dir: expected one repo from scope_to_repos, got {}",
904	            other.len()
905	        )
906	        .into()),
907	    }
908	}
909	
910	/// Resolve the bot repo of a workspace that *requires* one.
911	///
912	/// The dual-only sibling of [`bot_repo_path`] for operations that
913	/// make no sense without a bot side (push): `None` becomes a loud
914	/// error instead of a no-op signal.
915	pub fn require_bot_dir(workspace_root: &Path) -> Result<PathBuf, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
916	    bot_repo_path(workspace_root)?.ok_or_else(|| {
917	        format!(
918	            "{}'s config declares no bot repo (`repos.bot`): \
919	             this operation requires a dual workspace",
920	            workspace_root.display()
921	        )
922	        .into()
923	    })
924	}
925	
926	/// Dual-mode entry preflight: verify the two repos' recorded
927	/// topology agrees before any operation acts on it.
928	///
929	/// Checks, in order, erroring with everything known and changing
930	/// nothing (the dual-preflight principle, 2026-07-23):
931	///
932	/// - the bot dir exists (and is a directory);
933	/// - its `.vc-config.toml` loads;
934	/// - **resolved agreement**: each side's declared `[repos]` pair,
935	///   resolved file-relative and canonicalized, names the same two
936	///   directories (the file-relative schema makes the raw blocks
937	///   asymmetric by design, so agreement is checked on resolved
938	///   reality, not spelling);
939	/// - **self-identification**: each config's own directory sits at
940	///   its side's key (root's `work`, bot's `bot`): agreement
941	///   alone can't catch both sides naming the same wrong pair.
942	///
943	/// Mid-flight surprises stay per-operation concerns; this gates
944	/// *entry* at the one topology resolver.
945	fn verify_workspace_coherence(root: &Path, bot: &Path) -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
946	    if !bot.is_dir() {
947	        return Err(format!(
948	            "workspace incoherent: {}/.vc-config.toml declares bot repo '{}', \
949	             but that directory does not exist, fix the `bot` value or \
950	             restore the directory; nothing was changed",
951	            root.display(),
952	            bot.display()
953	        )
954	        .into());
955	    }
956	    let root_cfg = crate::config_md::load(root)?.ok_or_else(|| {
957	        format!(
958	            "workspace incoherent: no vc-x1 config found in '{}'; \
959	             nothing was changed",
960	            root.display()
961	        )
962	    })?;
963	    let bot_cfg = match crate::config_md::load(bot) {
964	        Ok(Some(cfg)) => cfg,
965	        Ok(None) => {
966	            return Err(format!(
967	                "workspace incoherent: bot repo '{}' has no vc-x1 config \
968	                 ({} or {VC_CONFIG_FILE}): both sides must carry a [repos] \
969	                 registry naming the same directories; nothing was changed",
970	                bot.display(),
971	                crate::config_md::VC_CONFIG_MD
972	            )
973	            .into());
974	        }
975	        Err(e) => {
976	            return Err(format!(
977	                "workspace incoherent: bot repo '{}' has no readable config \
978	                 ({e}): both sides must carry a [repos] registry naming the \
979	                 same directories; nothing was changed",
980	                bot.display()
981	            )
982	            .into());
983	        }
984	    };
985	    let (root_pair, bot_pair) = (
986	        resolved_repos_pair(root, &root_cfg)?,
987	        resolved_repos_pair(bot, &bot_cfg)?,
988	    );
989	    if root_pair != bot_pair {
990	        return Err(format!(
991	            "workspace incoherent: the two sides' [repos] registries resolve to \
992	             different directories: they must name the same work/bot pair; \
993	             nothing was changed\n\
994	             {}: work={}, bot={}\n\
995	             {}: work={}, bot={}",
996	            root_cfg.path.display(),
997	            root_pair.0.display(),
998	            root_pair.1.display(),
999	            bot_cfg.path.display(),
1000	            bot_pair.0.display(),
1001	            bot_pair.1.display()
1002	        )
1003	        .into());
1004	    }
1005	    // Self-identification: agreement alone can't catch both sides
1006	    // naming the same *wrong* pair: each config's own directory
1007	    // must sit at its side's key.
1008	    let canon_root = root.canonicalize()?;
1009	    if root_pair.0 != canon_root {
1010	        return Err(format!(
1011	            "workspace incoherent: {}'s `repos.work` resolves to \
1012	             '{}', not to the workspace root itself: the work side's own entry \
1013	             must name its own directory; nothing was changed",
1014	            root_cfg.path.display(),
1015	            root_pair.0.display()
1016	        )
1017	        .into());
1018	    }
1019	    let canon_bot = bot.canonicalize()?;
1020	    if bot_pair.1 != canon_bot {
1021	        return Err(format!(
1022	            "workspace incoherent: {}'s `repos.bot` resolves to \
1023	             '{}', not to the bot repo itself: the bot side's own entry must \
1024	             name its own directory; nothing was changed",
1025	            bot_cfg.path.display(),
1026	            bot_pair.1.display()
1027	        )
1028	        .into());
1029	    }
1030	    Ok(())
1031	}
1032	
1033	/// Resolve and canonicalize one side's declared `[repos]` pair.
1034	///
1035	/// The per-side half of the resolved-agreement check: reads
1036	/// `repos.work` / `repos.bot` from `cfg` (the config loaded at
1037	/// `cfg_dir`), resolves each file-relative, and canonicalizes:
1038	/// a missing key or unresolvable directory is its own coherence
1039	/// error.
1040	fn resolved_repos_pair(
1041	    cfg_dir: &Path,
1042	    cfg: &crate::config_md::VcConfig,
1043	) -> Result<(PathBuf, PathBuf), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
1044	    let resolve = |key: &str| -> Result<PathBuf, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
1045	        let value = toml_simple::toml_get(&cfg.map, key)
1046	            .filter(|v| !v.is_empty())
1047	            .ok_or_else(|| {
1048	                format!(
1049	                    "workspace incoherent: {} has no `{key}` in its \
1050	                     [repos] registry: both sides must declare the work/bot pair; \
1051	                     nothing was changed",
1052	                    cfg.path.display()
1053	                )
1054	            })?;
1055	        resolve_repo_path(cfg_dir, value)
1056	            .canonicalize()
1057	            .map_err(|e| {
1058	                format!(
1059	                    "workspace incoherent: {}'s `{key}` (\"{value}\") does \
1060	                 not resolve to an existing directory ({e}); nothing was changed",
1061	                    cfg.path.display()
1062	                )
1063	                .into()
1064	            })
1065	    };
1066	    Ok((resolve("repos.work")?, resolve("repos.bot")?))
1067	}
1068

#### Solution

Adopt a markdown carrier for the config surface (wink, 2026-08-11), then rebuild the pipeline
on it. The format: a config file is a markdown document whose `toml` fences, concatenated in
document order, form the TOML the loader parses, so prose, per-key doc, and real reference
links live beside the keys they document. `vc-config-test.md` is the model rendering
(compact: one fence per table, doc-link bullets above it).

- a md -> toml filter (non-fence lines blanked, so any diagnostics keep the source's line
  numbers) feeds the existing parser
  - the loader resolves `.vc-config.md`, still accepts `.vc-config.toml` for the family's
    migration window, and errors when a side has both
- the prototype `vc-config.toml` becomes `vc-config.md` in the same format: per-key `##`
  sections (the anchors the generated web urls land on) absorb `vc-config-design.md`, which
  retires, so the schema source and the browsable doc are one file

  `agent-session` subcommand and `--scope=agent`, with the old names rejected rather than
  aliased and the rejection printing its fix-it; the pinned prose sweep is a later convention
  cycle

  comment blocks and the `.vc-x1` state-dir leftovers
- `config --refresh` regenerates the prose between fences while preserving fence interiors
  and `[repos]` byte-for-byte
  - a `--check` mode renders and compares without writing, exiting nonzero on any
    difference, so a prototype edit that skipped the refresh fails loudly
- add a `validate-anchors` subcommand, the validate-repo design's first standalone slice:
  same-file heading anchors checked via the documented slug algorithm, plus `[N]` reference
  resolution, across the repo's markdown records
- per-key worked examples in `vc-config.md`, so a reference link rewards the click
- repoint `repos.agent` at `.agent-session`
  - the directory rename itself is wink's move between sessions (a live session writes
    through the symlink), with the following session committing the record

# Code conventions

Conventions for source code. Read this before writing code. The Rust-specific sections apply
wherever the medium is a Rust crate (see [custom.md](../custom.md) for the project's medium).

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Line width

Source lines, including doc comments and inline comments, wrap at the source width in
prose.md's [Line widths](prose.md#line-widths), which matches rustfmt's default `max_width`.
The per-commit flow's `cargo fmt` enforces it for code, and the same limit applies to the
comment text it doesn't reflow.

## Doc comments on every file, function, and method

Every `.rs` file must begin with a `//!` module docstring. Every function and method must have
a `///` doc comment. Keep them brief: one sentence of purpose is often enough. The discipline
is that the comment exists, not that it be long. Doc comments follow the
[Prose form](prose.md#prose-form) shape (intro + bullets).

This is a deliberate override of the generic "write no comments" default that applies to
inline `//` comments. Doc comments on the module / item surface are expected; inline
explanatory comments inside function bodies remain discouraged unless they capture a
non-obvious WHY.

**Clap-derive args:** doc comments on `#[arg(...)]` fields drive `--help` output. Clap reflows
by default and collapses bullets into running prose. Add `#[arg(verbatim_doc_comment, ...)]` on
any field whose doc comment uses bullets so each `- ...` lands on its own line in the rendered
help.

## `// OK: ...` comments on `unwrap*` calls (Rust)

The default in non-test code is to **not** use `.unwrap()`, `.expect(...)`, or the
`.unwrap_or*(...)` siblings. Prefer a shape that doesn't need them (`match`, `if let`, slice
patterns, infallible-by-construction APIs), which is usually also the clearer code. This is a
lean, not a ban: some sites are legitimately best expressed with one. Two kinds of risk, both
in scope:

- `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`: a panic path.
- `.unwrap_or(...)` / `.unwrap_or_default()` / `.unwrap_or_else(...)`: no panic, but a
  silently substituted value that can hide a wrong result.

When one is used, three obligations attach:

- A trailing `// OK: ...` comment justifying why the call is acceptable:
  - `// OK: <specific reason>`: document the real precondition, invariant, or domain reason.
    Preferred whenever the reason isn't self-evident.
  - `// OK: obvious`: the default is self-evident from context (e.g.
    `desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("")`, where an empty desc gives an empty title).
  - Bare `// OK` is not used (reads like a truncated comment). Abbreviations (e.g. `SE`) are
    not used because they require a decoder ring for readers seeing the code out of context.
- **Alert the user in conversation** when introducing one, so the site gets reviewed and
  appropriate uses are learned. Don't let it ride in silently on a larger diff.
- For `.unwrap()` / `.expect(...)`, an `#[allow(...)]` at the site, because Rust projects
  enable the project-wide lints in `Cargo.toml`:

  ```toml
  [lints.clippy]
  unwrap_used = "warn"
  expect_used = "warn"
  ```

  Every panicking site is then opt-in and visible in the diff, and clippy (in the per-commit
  flow) catches any that slip through. The `_or*` siblings have no clippy lint. They are covered
  by the comment convention and the conversational alert. (The template repository's
  `CargoRust.toml` seeds a base `Cargo.toml` with this section already in place.)

```rust
let max = stderr_level.unwrap_or(LevelFilter::Info); // OK: default verbosity when -v/-vv absent
let first_line = desc.lines().next().unwrap_or("");  // OK: obvious

match matches.len() {
    1 => {
        #[allow(clippy::unwrap_used)]
        // OK: `1 =>` arm guarantees matches.len() == 1
        Ok(TitleMatch::One(matches.into_iter().next().unwrap()))
    }
    // ...
}
```

Tests (`#[cfg(test)]`) are exempt, since panicking on setup failure is the correct test
behavior.

Fixed, tested, and verified against this workspace. The fix is in the working tree only — nothing committed, per the rules.

**The bug.** `validate-desc` (and `fix-desc`, which had the identical flaw) resolved "the other repo" by calling `bot_repo_path(&params.repo)`, a function whose contract says its argument is the *workspace root*. Run from the work repo that's accidentally true; run from `.claude`, the default `-R .` is the bot side, so the coherence preflight (added in `f8885f1 refactor: registry resolved-agreement preflight`) was handed the bot dir as "the root" and correctly reported that its `repos.work` doesn't name itself. The check was right; the caller was lying to it.

**The fix.** A new side-aware helper `other_repo_path()` in `src/common.rs:875` that both commands now call:

- It finds the workspace root *from* the given repo path (`find_workspace_root_from`, which already follows a bot-side config's `work = ".."` up to the real root), runs the existing coherence preflight against that true root, and returns the far side: the bot repo when you're on the work side, the work repo when you're in the bot repo. The bot check runs first via `starts_with`, since the bot dir nests inside the work repo. POR/single-repo still returns `None` for the no-op path, and legacy configs still reject.
- `bot_repo_path` itself is unchanged apart from its doc comment; its other callers (main.rs, version.rs, config_cmd.rs) all pass a real `find_workspace_root()` result.

No `unwrap`/`expect`/`unwrap_or` sites were introduced (rule 11: nothing to alert).

**Verification.** `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`, and `cargo test` all clean — 499 unit tests pass including three new ones for `other_repo_path` (from work side, from bot side — the regression case — and POR). End to end with the built binary: `validate-desc -R .claude @- 3` now reports `3 valid ... (of 3 total)`, and the work-side invocation is unchanged. Your original invocation (bare `validate-desc` from inside `.claude`) shows `@` as "miss", which is just the undescribed working-copy commit, not the bug.

Side notes from acquaint: the mailbox `../vc-x1-template/messages/vc-x1.md` has three open threads (the 2026-08-12 `.vc-config.md` feedback with the commit-body-form proposal being the newest) — untouched per your instruction. This fix would slot into the current `docs-freshen-vc-config-and-config-subcmd` cycle as a rung (it's fallout from the md-carrier work giving the bot side its own discoverable config), but I've left the ladder and TODO.md alone pending your say-so on where it lands.

The plain version: the command assumed it was always started from the main project folder. When you ran it from the `.claude` folder, it mistook that folder for the main one and the safety check rightly refused. It now works out which of the two folders it's in first, so both starting points work.

Agreed on the split, and yes — my miss too: I wrote the fix into a working copy that already carried your doc edits without flagging the mixing first. Thoughts on how I'd proceed, no actions taken:

**The good news: the two sets are perfectly file-disjoint.** Your doc edits are `.vc-config.md`, `TODO.md`, `custom-family.md`, `notes/todo-backlog.md`; the fix is entirely `src/` (common.rs, common/tests.rs, validate_desc.rs, fix_desc.rs). So a clean split is mechanical, with one wrinkle below.

**Order.** I'd land your doc changes first, then the fix. Reason: the fix becomes its own rung in the current cycle's ladder ("fix: validate-desc from the bot side", or similar — same species as the existing "fix: prompt double echo" and "fix: bot-session reads the md carrier" rungs), and per the protocol its commit should carry its own record edits: the ladder insertion in `TODO.md` and its `#####` section in the chores file. Those record edits land on top of whatever your pending `TODO.md` edits say, so your edits going first avoids me editing a file you have in flight. (I haven't read your four modified files yet; doing that would be step zero, since their content decides the doc commit's title and whether they're really one commit.)

**Mechanics, keeping rule 1 intact.** `vc-x1 push` commits the whole working copy, so one set has to be parked while the other pushes. Two ways:

1. **jj-native (my preference):** `jj split --parallel` the `src/` files into a *sibling* commit (a placeholder description, never published — the same category as rule 1's "work that never publishes"). Push your docs rung normally. Then `jj squash --from` the parked sibling into the new working copy, so the fix returns as ordinary uncommitted changes, and push the fix rung with `vc-x1 push` doing the describing and stamping as always. The placeholder dissolves; nothing pre-committed ever publishes.
2. **Low-tech fallback:** copy the four `src/` files to `tmp/`, `jj restore` them in the working copy, push docs, copy back, push fix. Zero jj cleverness, zero history residue, slightly inelegant.

Either way, each push gets its own moment-of-push approval from you (rule 2), fast validation runs before the fix rung's push, and the checklists get read before I touch anything.

**One open question for you:** the fix rung's records. I'd insert it in the ladder after "docs: config-surface records, bold backlog titles" and write its ladder-details section — but if your pending `TODO.md` edits already reorganize that area, tell me and I'll fit around them.

The plain version: your notes and my code fix touch completely different files, so pulling them apart is easy. I'd push your notes first, tuck my fix aside with a jj maneuver while that happens, then bring it back and push it as its own properly-recorded step — each push waiting for your ok.

content.text:
My recommendation: **option B, fix off main** — with a couple of things to verify before committing to it.

**Why B beats A:**

- **Conflict direction.** The pending "feat: agent naming in config and CLI" rung is going to rename exactly the identifiers the fix touches (`repos.bot`, `bot_repo_path`, the bot-side vocabulary). Under A, that rung doesn't know about the fix sitting above it, so *every* rebase of `fix-validate-desc` over the advancing branch means me hand-resolving my fix against the renames, repeatedly. Under B, the fix sits below: when docs-freshen rebases onto the new main, the rename rung just sweeps `other_repo_path`'s code along with everything else as ordinary development. Conflicts get paid once, and mostly dissolve.
- **ASAP actually means main.** The bug predates this cycle: the coherence preflight came in `f8885f1 refactor: registry resolved-agreement preflight`, which is pre-cycle, and the wrong-root call in validate-desc/fix-desc is older still — a toml-carrier bot config trips it the same way. So it's a genuine main bug, and B gets the fix into the installed plain `vc-x1` (and visible to the family) now, not at cycle end.
- **Structure.** Under A, `fix-validate-desc` carries the eleven docs-freshen commits beneath it, so it structurally *cannot* land on main first — landing it would land the unfinished docs cycle. It's really "part of the cycle with extra bookkeeping". B is a clean single-step cycle on its own bookmark off main, lands, bookmark deleted — rule 13 by the book.

**What B costs, and the caveats:**

1. **The patch must be re-verified against main's code state.** I wrote and tested it on branch state. The touched functions all exist on main and the fix logic is carrier-agnostic, so I expect it to apply with at most context drift in the tests — but that's an expectation, not a measurement. Full validation reruns on the main-based commit.
2. **End-to-end repro is weaker on main.** This workspace's on-disk configs are now md-carrier, which a main-built binary doesn't read, so the live repro would need a toml-carrier fixture; the new unit tests (from-bot-side is the regression case) carry the verification instead.
3. **The working-copy shuffle.** Your four doc edits stay parked on the docs-freshen tip (the current `@` just stays behind as a commit there); the `src/` diff moves to a fresh working copy on main via a duplicate/squash dance or a clean re-apply.
4. **One rebase of docs-freshen afterward.** The fix is an additive function plus two call-site swaps, so I'd expect trivial or no conflicts against the branch's config work — and the rebase rewrites the topic bookmark's commit ids (routine for an unlanded topic branch; descriptions untouched, so rule 4 isn't in play), meaning a force-push of the bookmark when it next publishes.

If verification in caveat 1 surprised us — the bug somehow not reproducible on main, or the patch depending on branch code — I'd fall back to A without argument, since then the fix genuinely belongs to the cycle.

The plain version: put the fix on its own little branch off main and merge it right away, then rebase the big in-progress branch on top once. The other order would mean re-fixing the same collisions over and over as the big branch grows, and the fix wouldn't reach the released tool until the whole branch finishes. First I'd double-check the fix still works against main as-is.

1	# Versioning
2	
3	How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
4	suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
5	copied **verbatim**, with
6	[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
7	conditional rather than per-project edits.
8	
9	Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
10	converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
11	Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).
12	
13	## Terms
14	
15	Three names, used as defined here across
16	[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
17	[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:
18	
19	- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
20	  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
21	  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
22	  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
23	  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
24	  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
25	- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
26	  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
27	  artifact derives from it.
28	- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.
29	
30	## A stamp, not a name
31	
32	The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
33	named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
34	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
35	suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
36	inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.
37	
38	## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides
39	
40	Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
41	touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**
42	
43	- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
44	  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
45	  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
46	  presentation, docs, notes.
47	- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
48	  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
49	- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
50	  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).
51	
52	**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
53	thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.
54	
55	## Grammar and storage
56	
57	One spelling everywhere the version is written:
58	
59	```
60	<public>[-<suffix>]
61	```
62	
63	- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
64	- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,
65	  `3.1`, `3.1.0`), with an alphanumeric id (`3.hotfix`) allowed sparingly.
66	- **Exactly one `-` in the whole version**, the one that opens the suffix: never a dash inside
67	  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
68	  version storable in every medium below.
69	- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
70	  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a leading `v`;
71	  Cargo rejects one.)
72	
73	Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:
74	
75	- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
76	  valid at any dot depth.
77	- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
78	  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
79	- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
80	  adds its case to
81	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).
82	
83	Two reservations keep the remap sound:
84

86	  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out); PEP 440 sorts the
87	  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
88	  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
89	  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
90	- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
91	  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
92	  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.
93	
94	**Why one dash, dots only:** a Python linter/formatter in a sibling repo rejected every
95	multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
96	2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
97	`+` are all invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but
98	silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
99	every medium accepts.
100	
101	## Recording the version-of-record
102	
103	Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
104	the case that fits your medium:
105	
106	- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
107	  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
108	  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
109	  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
110	    ...). Add the case as needed
111	- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
112	  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
113	  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
114	    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
115	- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
116	  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
117	  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
118	- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
119	  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
120	  per-commit preference.
121	
122	## Dev artifact name
123	
124	When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
125	active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
126	clobbers the binary consumers are running:
127	
128	- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
129	  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
130	  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
131	- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
132	  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
133	  install dir with stale binaries.
134	- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
135	  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
136	  flow's install.
137	
138	Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
139	its `custom.md` layer.
140	
141	## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)
142	
143	Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
144	running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.
145	
146	- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
147	  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
148	  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
149	- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
150	  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
151	  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).
152	
153	## Suffix scheme
154	
155	The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
156	each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.
157	
158	This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
159	not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
160	neither a number nor a version (see
161	[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
162	prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
163	commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
164	nothing dereferences one.
165	
166	- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
167	- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
168	- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)
169	
170	**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
171	and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
172	Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
173	without renumbering siblings.
174	
175	Disambiguation:
176	
177	- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
178	- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).
179	
180	**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:
181	
182	- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
183	- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
184	- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
185	- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle
186	
187	Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
188	step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
189	above, every commit carries a distinct version.

# Versioning

How this project versions its commits and the running artifact. The scheme, meaning the cycle
suffix spelling and the unique-per-commit aim, is generic and shared across projects: this file is
copied **verbatim**, with
[Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) covering each medium by
conditional rather than per-project edits.

Universal file, shared with the template repository. A proposed change is edited here and
converges at the template ([Changing the agent-files](../AGENTS.md#changing-the-agent-files)).
Project-local content goes in [custom.md](../custom.md).

## Terms

Three names, used as defined here across
[AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md),
[cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md), and the notes files:

- **version**: the per-commit version (e.g. `0.3.0-5.3.0`). It lives in the manifest. No
  ladder, todo entry, commit title, or commit body writes one, the one exception being the
  chores as-built rung recording a landed commit (see
  [Versions live in the version-of-record only](prose.md#versions-live-in-the-version-of-record-only)),
  and its suffix encodes the cycle phase for whoever inspects the manifest (see
  [Suffix scheme](#suffix-scheme)).
- **version-of-record**: the authoritative stored copy of the version, in the project's manifest
  (see [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record)). A built or running
  artifact derives from it.
- **versioning**: the topic, this scheme as a whole.

## A stamp, not a name

The version answers "which commit produced this artifact". It is not a name for a step: a step is
named by its title and located by its position in the ladder list (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). So the
suffix below is the only number in the system, and since nothing dereferences it, reordering or
inserting a step leaves the versions already committed alone.

## Advancing X.Y.Z: scope decides

Which of the three numbers moves is decided by the **scope of the change**, not by whether it
touched code: **minor for architecture, patch for everything else.**

- The test is whether the *shape* of the system changed or only its contents. Minor when the
  structure moves: a subsystem added or removed, a pipeline reshaped, an output contract
  redesigned. Patch for work within the existing shape: incremental features, new cases,
  presentation, docs, notes.
- **A docs-only change can be a minor** and a large code change can be a patch. Volume is not
  scope, and the earlier functional-versus-docs test kept getting this backwards.
- **Major is a project's own call**, since what `X` promises depends on the artifact and its
  users. The project records that promise in [custom.md](../custom.md).

**Why:** the suffix already encodes a commit's phase, so `X.Y.Z` is free to encode the only other
thing a reader wants from a version at a glance, how big a change they are looking at.

## Grammar and storage

One spelling everywhere the version is written:

```
<public>[-<suffix>]
```

- `<public>`: `X.Y.Z`, integers.
- `<suffix>`: dot-separated identifiers, each ASCII letters or digits: usually integers (`3`,

  the suffix, never a `+` in this spelling. This is the portability invariant that makes the
  version storable in every medium below.
- **`v` is a display prefix, not part of the version**: conversation and reports may write
  `v0.78.0-3.1` for scannability; manifests store the bare form. (PEP 440 ignores a leading `v`;
  Cargo rejects one.)

Storage is a per-medium remap of that one spelling:

- **SemVer mediums** (Rust/Cargo): store verbatim. The suffix rides in the prerelease slot,
  valid at any dot depth.
- **PEP 440 mediums** (Python): remap the single `-` to `+`: `0.78.0-3.1` -> `0.78.0+3.1`.
  Mechanical and bijective because there is exactly one dash to find.
- **Other mediums**: verbatim if the format allows the one `-`, else the `+` remap. A new medium
  adds its case to
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record).

Two reservations keep the remap sound:

- **The stored version identifies; it does not order.** SemVer sorts a suffixed version *before*
  its bare release (matching cycle semantics: rungs precede close-out); PEP 440 sorts the
  remapped form *after* it, and reinterprets a lone `-N` as a post-release. Opposite directions,
  so no cross-medium logic may compare stored versions. Ordering truth lives in the ladder and
  git history. Comparing the public triple alone (e.g. a version gate) is unaffected.
- **`+` is reserved** for the PEP 440 remap: no SemVer build-metadata use in Rust repos even
  though Cargo allows it, since spending `+` there breaks the bijection with the Python
  spelling. A repo that truly needs it declares the deviation in its `custom.md`.

multi-dash version outright, and the PEP 440 reference parser (`packaging` 26.2, tested
2026-07-30) confirms the boundary: `1.2.3-3.1`, `1.2.3-x+ab+cd`, `1.2.3-34-abc`, and any second
`+` are all invalid; `1.2.3+3.1` / `1.2.3+3.1.hotfix` parse at any depth; `1.2.3-1` parses but
silently becomes the post-release `1.2.3.post1`. The one-dash dotted grammar is the largest form
every medium accepts.

## Recording the version-of-record

Where the version-of-record lives, how it's stored and surfaced, and how often it changes. Pick
the case that fits your medium:

- **Manifest**, where the version-of-record is stored:
  - if Rust, `Cargo.toml` `[package].version`
  - if Python, `pyproject.toml` `[project].version` (or the committed config it's sourced from)
  - otherwise wherever the medium records it (a generic `version.toml`, a book's frontmatter,
    ...). Add the case as needed
- **Notation**, how the `-` form is stored. See [Grammar and storage](#grammar-and-storage):
  - if the format allows `-` (TOML `version.toml`, `Cargo.toml`), store it verbatim
  - if it bars `-` (PEP 440's local segment, e.g. a Python project), remap to `+`, so
    `0.3.0-5.3.0` becomes `0.3.0+5.3.0`: same version, just the stored spelling
- **Reporter**, how a built artifact surfaces the version-of-record:
  - if a CLI app, `<cli-app> -V`
  - if a TUI/GUI, add to Help/About or display on the title
- **Cadence**, how often to bump: see
  [Unique per commit](#unique-per-commit-preference-not-requirement). This project follows the
  per-commit preference.

## Dev artifact name

When other projects consume the built artifact (e.g. the installed CLI) while this repo is under
active development, the dev build installs under a separate name so a mid-cycle install never
clobbers the binary consumers are running:

- **Name**: the manifest's package name carries a `-dev` suffix (`<name>` -> `<name>-dev`). If
  Rust, `[package].name`, so the per-commit flow's `cargo install` produces `<name>-dev` and
  leaves plain `<name>` untouched.
- **Constant, not per-step**: the step already lives in the version-of-record (`<name>-dev -V`
  reports the exact rung). A per-step name would churn the manifest every commit and litter the
  install dir with stale binaries.
- **Promotion**: plain `<name>` updates only by an explicit act: a separate clone built at the
  chosen commit with the plain name (or a copy of the dev binary), never by the per-commit
  flow's install.

Projects without external consumers can skip it. A project that adopts it records the fact in
its `custom.md` layer.

## Unique per commit (preference, not requirement)

Our general notion is that the version-of-record should change on **every commit**, so a built or
running artifact identifies the exact commit it came from.

- This is a preference, **not** a hard requirement. A project following the cycle protocol may
  bump less often: once per cycle, only at release, and so on. Record the choice in
  [Recording the version-of-record](#recording-the-version-of-record) if it differs.
- It is achievable because the cycle's versions (below) are **pre-assignable**, unlike the git
  SHA, which a commit cannot contain (see the cycle protocol's
  [Commits backfill](cycle-protocol.md#commits-backfill)).

## Suffix scheme

The cycle (Preparation -> Work -> Close-out, per [cycle-protocol.md](cycle-protocol.md)) encodes
each commit's phase in the version suffix, the **final identifier `0` marking a Preparation**.

This is the manifest's own spelling, read by whoever inspects `Cargo.toml` or `-V` output. It is
not a name for a step: a step is identified by its title, and an in-flight ladder rung carries
neither a number nor a version (see
[Steps are named, not numbered](prose.md#steps-are-named-not-numbered)). The one
prose surface that records a version is a chores as-built rung, where it is a property of a landed
commit sitting beside that commit's SHA. The identifiers below count commits within a phase, and
nothing dereferences one.

- `X.Y.Z-0`: Preparation
- `X.Y.Z-1`, `X.Y.Z-2`, ...: Work commits
- `X.Y.Z`: Close-out (bare version, no suffix)

**Preparation is optional.** A lightweight cycle, with no ladder and no setup commit, skips `-0`
and starts at `-1` (its first Work commit). The same holds at every level: a sub-cycle needing no
Preparation omits its `.0` (see Nesting). One that grows a Preparation later adds the `0` step
without renumbering siblings.

Disambiguation:

- `-10`: Work commit #10 (final identifier `10`), not a Preparation.
- `-1.0`: Preparation of the `-1` sub-cycle (final identifier `0`).

**Nesting.** Sub-cycles append another level, recursively:

- `X.Y.Z-3.0`: Preparation of the `-3` sub-cycle
- `X.Y.Z-3.1`, `X.Y.Z-3.2`: its Work
- `X.Y.Z-3`: its Close-out
- `X.Y.Z-3.1.0`: Preparation of the `-3.1` sub-sub-cycle

Bump the version-of-record at the start of every step (the per-commit checklist carries the
step), so the manifest always records the commit it will be part of and, per the preference
above, every commit carries a distinct version.

content.text:
Grounded in versioning.md now. Ranking the options:

**Reject `0.78.7-fix-validate-desc`.** The bare `0.78.7` close-out already exists on main, and the scheme's suffix semantics say a suffixed version is a *rung preceding its close-out* (SemVer even sorts it before `0.78.7`). So that spelling reads as a work commit of an already-closed cycle — a stamp that misidentifies, which is the one job the version has.

**Your full-renumber option works but is heavy.** Rebasing `0.78.8-0..-10` into `0.78.9-N` (or `0.79.0-N`) means editing eleven commits' `Cargo.toml` *and* `Cargo.lock` (the lock records the package's own version, so it churned every rung), plus the chores as-built entries on the branch that recorded landed versions beside SHAs — those would now be false and live inside the commits that wrote them. Each rewritten commit's recorded validation also goes stale. One real comfort: ochid trailers carry jj change ids, which survive rewrites, so cross-repo links hold. Still, that's a lot of surgery for cosmetic uniformity of the branch's own stamps.

**My recommendation: a forward-only renumber.** The fix cycle claims **0.78.8** — the next free triple off main, and patch scope fits a bugfix. As a single-step cycle its one commit is the close-out, so it stamps bare `0.78.8`. The docs-freshen branch then renumbers *from here on*: already-landed rungs keep their committed `0.78.8-N` stamps untouched (nothing dereferences a suffix; ordering truth lives in the ladder and history — versioning.md is explicit that the stored version identifies, it does not order), and the remaining rungs continue as `0.79.0-11` onward with the close-out landing as bare `0.79.0`, plus a one-line note in the cycle's records at the renumber beat. Main stays monotonic: 0.78.7 → 0.78.8 (fix) → 0.79.0 (docs). No history rewrite beyond the rebase B already entails, no per-commit edits.

The leftover blemish is that the branch's early rungs say `0.78.8-N` while `0.78.8` ends up being the fix release. Amusingly, SemVer ordering (`0.78.8-N` before `0.78.8`) matches wall-clock truth — those rungs *did* precede the fix landing — it's only the "rung of that cycle" implication that's off, and the records note covers it.

**One genuine judgment call for you: `0.78.9` vs `0.79.0` for the docs cycle's remainder.** Scope decides, minor for architecture — and this cycle reshapes the config pipeline (md carrier, build.rs codegen, `repos.bot` → `repos.agent` schema rename, new subcommands). That reads as structure moving, not contents, so I'd lean **0.79.0**. The cycle originally claiming a patch triple was arguably under-scoped from the start, and this renumber is a natural moment to correct it.

And the fourth option nobody proposed — fix takes 0.78.9, docs keeps 0.78.8 and lands later — I'd reject: the installed binary's version would go backwards when docs closes, which is needless confusion even if the scheme technically permits it.

The plain version: don't reuse or suffix the already-released number, and don't rewrite eleven commits to renumber the branch. Give the fix the free number 0.78.8, and have the big branch simply switch to the next number (I'd pick 0.79.0, since that branch is a big structural change) for its remaining commits, leaving its old stamps alone with a short note in the records.

Plan for phase 1, with the stop points and the surprises I'm already watching for:

**Sequence.**

1. **Read the checklists first** (cycle-checklists, the protocol's single-step folding, notes.md for the records edits) — rule 7 before any commit work.
2. **Verify the bug on main before anything else.** B's premise is that this is a main bug. I'll build main and reproduce against a toml-carrier fixture. If it doesn't reproduce there — stop, talk.
3. **The shuffle.** Save the `src/` diff aside, `jj restore` those four files in the current `@`, so your doc edits remain parked as the (undescribed) working-copy commit on docs-freshen, untouched until the rebase. Then `jj new main`, new bookmark `fix-validate-desc`, re-apply the fix. Cargo.toml comes back as main's (plain `vc-x1`, 0.78.7); set version `0.78.8` bare, since the single commit *is* the close-out.
4. **Records.** The fix cycle's records (chores section, done entry) get written against main's versions of those files — deliberately, since that's where the cycle lives. This guarantees TODO.md/chores conflicts at the later rebase; accepted and expected, we'll resolve them then.
5. **Full validation** (fmt, clippy, test, install — close-out makes it mandatory), then **stop for your approval before the push** (rule 2), push the rung to the topic bookmark, and after your test, landing on main is its own approved step, then bookmark deletion.
6. **Release as `vc-x1`.** Off main the package name should already be plain `vc-x1`, so `cargo install --path . --locked` at the fix commit produces exactly the release binary — versioning.md's "explicit act" of promotion, which your instruction authorizes. It clobbers the `vc-x1` you're running; that's the point, but I'll say so at the moment I do it.

**Surprises I can already see, in likelihood order:**

- **You may not be able to test it in *this* workspace.** The on-disk instance configs here have migrated to `.vc-config.md`, which a main-era binary doesn't read — a 0.78.8 `vc-x1` here would likely see a POR, not the dual workspace, and the repro-from-`.claude` needs a config to find. I'll check what's actually on disk (whether any `.vc-config.toml` survives) and report; worst case your test happens in a toml-carrier workspace or a scratch fixture I set up for you.
- **Patch drift.** The fix was written and tested on branch state. The functions it touches all exist on main and the logic is carrier-agnostic, but the surrounding code differs (the branch rewrote config loading), so I expect at least test-fixture drift. Small drift I'll just fix; if the port turns into a rewrite — stop, talk.
- **The build.rs name guard.** custom-family says build.rs guards the name on every cargo verb, plain `vc-x1` on main, dev names on long-lived branches. I don't know yet how it treats a short-lived topic bookmark carrying the plain name. I'll read build.rs before building; if it fights the plain-name build on `fix-validate-desc` — stop, talk, since the workaround choice (build at the landed main commit vs. adjust the guard) is yours.

Per your instruction, anything on that list that actually bites becomes a conversation, not an improvisation. Phase 2 (renumber docs-freshen to 0.79.0-N forward-only and rebase) waits until your test passes and the fix has landed.

The plain version: I'll first prove the bug exists on plain main, then move the fix onto a fresh little branch off main with version 0.78.8, write up its records, run the full checks, and pause for your ok before anything publishes. Then I build and install it as the real `vc-x1` for you to test — warning: you may need to test it somewhere still using the old config format, since this project's config files have already moved to the new one the old code can't read. Rebasing the big branch waits until after your test.
